## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Padumajātaka* (Ja 261), translated as *The Lotus*, belongs to the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework recorded at Jetavana, the Buddha delivered the story concerning several monks who presented offerings of garlands beneath "Ānanda’s tree" [SuttaCentral]. This tree, renowned across India, had been planted by the elder Ānanda near the gate of Jetavana; the contextual backstory is cross-referenced to the *Kāliṅgabodhi-jātaka* ("Kalinga-bodhi Birth") [SuttaCentral]. The canonical core opens with the verse phrase, "Cut, and cut, and cut again" [SuttaCentral]. In modern studies, Oskar von Hinüber indexes Ja 261 in reference to textual variants cited within the tradition [von Hinüber 1996].

SuttaCentral records four modern translations across four languages, with no curated canonical parallels [SuttaCentral]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus identifies substantial Pali-internal correspondence between the *Padumajātaka* and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), consisting of seven matching passages (663 shared characters), with the longest match spanning segments §1.1–2.4 [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language automated alignments, DharmaNexus detects six matches with a Tibetan Kangyur text (BO_K01_D0005_H0005, e.g., segment §0.3 matching §95b-20 with scores up to 35), though these machine-generated alignments remain unconfirmed by SuttaCentral [DharmaNexus].
